[TradingView](https://in.tradingview.com/?aff_id=167054) vs Thinkorswim comparison is a hot topic among traders who want the best platform for charting, analysis, and execution. Both tools enjoy strong followings, but they serve slightly different needs. In this guide we’ll break down the strengths, weaknesses, and ideal use‑cases of each so you can decide which one fits your trading style.

## Overview
TradingView started as a web‑based charting service and grew into a full‑featured social trading network. Thinkorswim, owned by TD Ameritrade (now Charles Schwab), is a desktop‑centric platform aimed at active traders who need deep analytics and direct market access. While both offer powerful charting, their ecosystems differ in pricing, broker integration, and community feel.

## Key Features
### Real‑time Data
TradingView provides free delayed data for many exchanges, with paid plans unlocking real‑time US equities, futures, and crypto. Thinkorswim includes real‑time streaming for all supported assets at no extra cost, assuming you have a funded brokerage account.

### Technical Indicators
Both platforms ship with over 100 built‑in studies. TradingView’s Pine Script lets you create custom indicators and strategies that run in the cloud. Thinkorswim’s thinkScript offers similar flexibility but requires the desktop client and is tighter‑coupled to the broker’s data feed.

### Drawing Tools
TradingView excels at intuitive drawing tools—trendlines, Fibonacci, pitchforks, and annotation shapes are drag‑and‑drop easy. Thinkorswim offers a comparable set, though the interface feels more utilitarian and less polished for quick sketching.

### Order Execution
Thinkorswim shines here: you can route orders directly to multiple exchanges, set complex conditional orders, and access level II quotes. TradingView recently added broker‑linked trading via partners (e.g., Tradier, Forex.com), but order types remain more basic than Thinkorswim’s advanced suite.

## Charting & Analysis
### Chart Types
TradingView supports candlestick, bar, line, Heikin‑Ashi, Renko, Kagi, point‑and‑figure, and more—all fully customizable. Thinkorswim covers the major types but lacks some niche options like Kagi and point‑and‑figure without third‑party add‑ons.

### Multi‑Chart Layouts
Both allow multiple charts per screen. TradingView’s web layout feels fluid, letting you sync symbols across panels with a click. Thinkorswim’s workspace system is powerful but can feel cluttered for newcomers.

### Backtesting
Thinkorswim’s onDemand feature lets you replay historical tick data and test strategies intraday. TradingView’s Pine Script backtesting is robust for end‑of‑day data; intraday backtesting requires a paid plan and external data feeds.

## Broker Integration
Thinkorswim is tightly integrated with TD Ameritrade/Charles Schwab accounts, giving you seamless fund transfers, margin monitoring, and retail‑focused research. TradingView remains broker‑agnostic; you connect via supported brokers or use its own paper trading mode. If you already have a Schwab account, Thinkorswim eliminates extra logins.

## Pricing Plans
TradingView offers a free tier with limited indicators and one chart per layout. Paid plans start at $14.95/month (Pro), $29.95/month (Pro+), and $49.95/month (Premium), scaling with more alerts, server‑side Pine Script execution, and data privileges. Thinkorswim is free to use if you hold a funded TD Ameritrade/Schwab account; otherwise, you must open a brokerage account to access the platform. There are no subscription fees, but you may incur commissions or fees based on your broker’s schedule.

## Ease of Use
### Learning Curve
TradingView’s clean, modern UI makes it approachable for beginners; tutorials and community scripts lower the barrier. Thinkorswim’s desktop client packs a lot of power, which can overwhelm new users initially, though the built‑in help and paperMoney simulator ease the transition.

### Mobile Experience
Both platforms have iOS/Android apps. TradingView’s mobile app mirrors the web experience closely, offering full charting and alert capabilities. Thinkorswim’s mobile app focuses on account management and basic charting; advanced analysis is still best done on desktop.

## Community & Support
TradingView boasts a vibrant public script library, idea publishing, and chat rooms where traders share setups. Thinkorswim relies more on official support channels, webinars, and the thinkorswim community forum, which is helpful but less socially driven.

## Final Verdict
Choose TradingView if you value flexible cloud‑based charting, enjoy sharing ideas, and want a platform that works anywhere without a brokerage tie‑in. Opt for Thinkorswim if you need direct order routing, advanced backtesting, and already trade with TD Ameritrade/Charles Schwab—or plan to do so. Many traders actually use both: TradingView for ideation and Thinkorswim for execution.
